extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write and read mathematical proofs; instructors of introductory proof courses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, definitions, and pedagogical notes for teaching and learning introductory mathematical proof techniques and set-theoretic foundations; includes notation conventions, examples, and an instructor timetable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a set and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is a collection of things; the things in the collection are called elements of the set. Sets are often written by listing elements between braces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: {2,4,6,8}; sets may have infinitely many elements (e.g., the integers ...,-2,-1,0,1,2,...). Emphasize that elements are the items in the 'box' representation of a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sets are equal if they contain exactly the same elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order and repetition do not matter: {2,4,6,8} = {4,2,8,6}. Counterexample: {2,4,6,8} ≠ {2,4,6,7}. Use this as a correctness criterion when comparing sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use x ∈ A to denote 'x is an element of A' and x ∉ A for 'x is not an element of A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may list multiple memberships like 6,2 ∈ A. Use uppercase letters for sets (A,B, ...).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite vs infinite sets and cardinality
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is finite, its cardinality |X| is the number of elements it has. A set is infinite if it has infinitely many elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: |{2,4,6,8}| = 4, |∅| = 0. Cardinality is used throughout to count and compare sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty set vs set containing the empty set (notation care)
rubrics_metrics.description: The empty set ∅ is the set with no elements; do not write {∅} when you mean ∅ because {∅} contains one element (the empty set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: confusing ∅ and {∅}. Use the 'box' analogy: ∅ is an empty box; {∅} is a box containing an empty box. Cardinalities differ (0 vs 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-builder notation syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets too large or complex to list are written as {expression : rule}, read 'the set of all things of form expression such that rule holds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colon may be replaced by a vertical bar in some texts. Examples: E = {2n : n ∈ Z} or {x ∈ R : x^2 − 2 = 0}. Show multiple equivalent forms for the same set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish absolute value vs cardinality notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbol |X| denotes absolute value when X is a number and cardinality when X is a set; the meaning should be clear from context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example ambiguity: |x| when x ∈ Z means absolute value; |X| when X is a set means cardinality. Check context to avoid misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard special sets and their notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve standard symbols for common sets: N for natural numbers, Z for integers, Q for rationals (m/n where m,n ∈ Z, n ≠ 0), R for real numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind students of relationships (N ⊆ Z ⊆ Q ⊆ R) and that Q ≠ R (e.g., √2 ∉ Q but ∈ R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interval notation definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define closed [a,b], half-open (a,b], [a,b), open (a,b), and infinite intervals (a,∞), [a,∞), (−∞,b), (−∞,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize these denote sets with infinitely many elements and clarify the possible notational collision of (a,b) meaning both an interval and an ordered pair in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered pair definition and order importance
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered pair is a list (x,y) of two things; order matters, so (2,4) ≠ (4,2) in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordered pairs need not be numbers; can be letters, sets, or ordered pairs themselves. Use when describing points in the plane or tuples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given sets A and B, A × B = { (a,b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B } (the set of ordered pairs from A and B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and visual aids: draw elements of A horizontally and B vertically to form the product; (R × R) is the Cartesian plane. For finite sets, |A × B| = |A|·|B|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting principle for Cartesian products
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are finite sets then |A × B| = |A| · |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rectangular array visualization. Generalize to n-fold products: |A1 × ... × An| = ∏ |Ai| for finite factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian powers and tuple vs nested-pair caution
rubrics_metrics.description: An becomes A × A × ... × A (n times). Distinguish (x,(y,z)) from (x,y,z); many texts blur them but conceptually they differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of parentheses when factors themselves are Cartesian products; it's usually harmless to identify them but be precise when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsets definition and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ B means every element of A is also an element of B; A ⊄ B means A is not a subset of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalize by checking elements; examples illustrate membership vs subset distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty set is subset of every set (Fact 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set B, ∅ ⊆ B because there is no element of ∅ that can violate subset property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain via 'select nothing' from B when constructing subsets; use this as a standard fact used in proofs and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of subsets of a finite set (Fact 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a finite set has n elements, then it has 2^n subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate via binary choices (insert or not insert each element) and tree diagrams; use when counting power sets or applying combinatorial reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree method for listing subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: List all subsets by branching for each element: at each step choose to include or exclude an element, generating 2^n outcomes for n elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a constructive enumeration technique and pedagogical device to teach power set counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish membership (∈) from subset (⊆)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object X may be an element of a set B (X ∈ B) or a subset of B (X ⊆ B); these are different relations and often both can be true for different X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples (e.g., 1 ∈ {1,{1}} but 1 ⊄ {1,{1}}; {1} ∈ {{1}} and {1} ⊆ {1} are different facts) to avoid common student confusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use braces to list elements, elements need not be numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets need not contain numbers; elements can be letters, points, matrices, or even other sets, and are listed inside braces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: B = {T,F}, C = {a,e,i,o,u}, M = {matrices}. Emphasize interpretation of entries when elements are themselves sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization advice for set concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use box analogies for sets, rectangular arrays for Cartesian products, and drawings for geometric subsets (e.g., unit circle ⊆ R^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual aids help clarify abstract distinctions (e.g., ∅ vs {∅}) and to understand subsets, products, graphs, and intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care when comparing different mathematical objects of similar form
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects that look similar (e.g., the set of 2×3 matrices M and R^6) are not identical; they may be in bijection but remain conceptually different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the set of 2×3 real matrices is similar to R^6 but not equal; encourage precision in identifying mathematical types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor course design guidance (timetable and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book is designed for a three-credit course with a suggested 14-week timetable; sections marked with * may require only brief mention or be left for self-study; some instructors may omit Chapter 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided weekly schedule as a flexible syllabus template; adapt by omitting or briefly treating starred sections based on course needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/publishing policy for the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisions or new editions will be issued only to correct mistakes and clarify exposition; new exercises may be added but existing ones will not be unnecessarily changed or renumbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets expectations for instructors and adopters about stability of exercise numbering and the purpose of updates.
